notes: \cpara{Retells the story of the author's teenage theory, first told in ``My Wild and Reckless Youth'' (2007) and again the day before in ``When Science Can't Help'' (see the notes there). The theory itself is still not described; this post needs only that it had experimental consequences and was professed testable.}
\cpara{Says that this was all the virtue the young author had been taught to require.}
\cpara{Says it was nowhere near the effort needed to get the theory right.}
\cpara{The charge against the traditional ideal: anyone who tests a theory and accepts the result has played by the rules, and even a negative result counts as knowledge.}
\cpara{Adds that playing by the rules is not the same as getting it right.}

\cpara{Limits the claim to the ideal ``as it is traditionally preached,'' not the practice of science, and gives two reasons. The post quotes no text that states the ideal. A commenter, poke, objected in the comments that this ideal is ``a second-hand imprecise (idealized) description of science,'' a ``philosophical model'' that is not ``used (or aimed for) within science.'' The next post answers another part of the same comment.}

\cpara{Explains why the ideal leaves the choice of hypothesis to the scientist: a rule for choosing would need the armchair reasoning that Science rebelled against. The split between how a hypothesis is found and how it is tested is the one philosophers discuss as Reichenbach's contexts of discovery and justification (see the note on ``When Science Can't Help'').}
\cpara{Grants that this minimal demand is enough for science to progress, slowly, perhaps only as a generation of elders dies out.}
\cpara{Sums up: Science asks only that you accept reality when it hits you.}

\cpara{The contrast: probability theory gives one exact answer. The arithmetic checks. True positives are $0.01 \times 0.8 = 0.008$ and false positives $0.99 \times 0.1 = 0.099$, so the answer is $0.008/0.107 \approx 7.48\%$, which is 7.5\% to one decimal. In this example the prior, 1\%, is given; the harder case, where no one gives it, comes later in the post.}
\cpara{Quotes the third virtue, lightness, from the author's own ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' (2006). The quotation matches that text.}
\cpara{Restates the ideal: you may believe and test any hypothesis that experiment has not ruled out, and Science gives no official verdict on which is best to test.}

\clogic{Karl Popper, the tradition's best-known modern voice, did rank hypotheses before testing, but by content, not probability. In the Stanford Encyclopedia's summary, for Popper ``the more improbable a theory is the better it is scientifically, because the probability and informative content of a theory vary inversely.'' So the tradition does contain a criterion applied before the test; it favours bold theories rather than probable ones.}
\cpara{Says that within the bounds of the evidence, Science lets you wander as you please.}
\cpara{Says this does not fit Bayesianism's single ``exactly right'' estimate, nor Science's founding distrust of individual reasoning; perfect Bayesians would need no social process of science.}

\cpara{Tells how, around the time of the mistake, the author found a stricter standard in Kahneman, Tversky and Jaynes, one that could have said in advance that the hypothesis was a poor choice. The author's 2007 account of the switch names the same sources, with Laplace (``The Importance of Saying Oops'').}
\cpara{Grants that Bayes is much harder to use: it needs you to hear ``tiny false notes'' where Science needs you only to notice an anvil.}
\cpara{Says that under Science a later experiment corrects your mistakes, at worst after a couple of decades.}
\cpara{Says that reasoning without overwhelming evidence is like mathematics: one error in a hundred steps can lead anywhere.}
\cpara{Grants that Science has good reason not to trust individuals with this, and to ask for experimental proof even after someone says they have reasoned out the answer.}
\cpara{Concludes that someone who does not want to waste ten years must attempt the harder task anyway.}

\cpara{Here the post takes one side of a dispute among Bayesians and does not mention the other. In the Stanford Encyclopedia's account (``Bayesian Epistemology''), subjective Bayesians such as de Finetti and Savage hold ``that every prior is permitted unless it fails to be coherent,'' while objective Bayesians, Jaynes among them, add a further norm for priors. The point is made in full in the note on ``My Wild and Reckless Youth.''}

\cpara{Argues that if priors chosen by whim gave correct estimates, a mind could know things without looking. That is true of accuracy. The subjective school's claim, as the Encyclopedia states it, is about what is ``permitted,'' not about what is accurate, and the paragraph does not address it.}

\cpara{Says that a Bayesian answer exists even when it is hard to compute, because Bayes is ``the law'' behind every method. This is the thesis of ``Beautiful Probability,'' whose notes find its claims of coherence and optimality stated more broadly than the results behind them.}
\cpara{Grants that no one knows how to do Bayesian inference over all possible theories in practice, but says that human guesses do not therefore break the laws of probability.}

\cpara{Credits the commenter Nick Tarleton with the clearest statement of the point. The quotation matches the comment, which also defends the lax social standard: ``Surely this is a good thing, else fear of being thought stupid would overly discourage people from raising novel hypotheses.''}
